overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of Bergson's account of time. You'll be asked about qualitative and quantitative multiplicity, spatialized time, duration, the body as center of action, and habit and pure memory.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: Why does Bergson think that counting always involves space?

options.html: Because only physical objects can be counted at all
options.text: Because only physical objects can be counted at all
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Bergson allows that we count abstract units too. His point is that we still set them out side by side in an ideal space.

options.html: Because identical units stay distinct only by position
options.text: Because identical units stay distinct only by position
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! To count, units must be treated as identical yet kept distinct, and only position in an ideal space keeps them apart.

options.html: Because numbers are written down on paper or screens
options.text: Because numbers are written down on paper or screens
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The point isn't about notation. Identical units can stay distinct only by occupying different positions in an ideal space.

options.html: Because the brain stores numbers in spatial regions
options.text: Because the brain stores numbers in spatial regions
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Bergson's argument isn't about the brain. It's that identical units stay distinct only by position in an ideal space.

forms.stemHtml: A musician holds one note of a familiar tune too long. On Bergson's account, how does a listener notice the mistake?

options.html: By measuring the extra length of the note against the beat
options.text: By measuring the extra length of the note against the beat
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Bergson argues we don't notice the excess length as length. We notice a change in the quality of the whole phrase.

options.html: By counting the notes and finding one extra unit
options.text: By counting the notes and finding one extra unit
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. No note is added. The listener notices a change in the quality of the whole phrase.

options.html: By hearing a change in the quality of the whole phrase
options.text: By hearing a change in the quality of the whole phrase
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Because the notes interpenetrate, a change in one part changes the whole, which shows that the melody is a qualitative multiplicity.

options.html: By comparing the note with a memory of each separate note
options.text: By comparing the note with a memory of each separate note
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Bergson's point is that the listener hears a change in the quality of the whole phrase.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following describe duration, in Bergson's sense? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: Lived time as a qualitative flow
options.text: Lived time as a qualitative flow
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Duration is lived time as a qualitative flow.
Correct! In duration, moments interpenetrate, each coloring the next.
Correct! Duration is succession without the distinct, side-by-side units of spatialized time.
Sorry, that's incorrect. That's spatialized time, which Bergson calls space in disguise.

options.html: Time that feels as if it passes quickly
options.text: Time that feels as if it passes quickly
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Duration concerns how moments relate, not how fast time seems to pass.

forms.stemHtml: You learn a poem by reading it aloud many times, and now you can recite it without recalling any particular reading. What is Bergson's term for this form of memory? Enter two words.

options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Habit memory is stored in the body as an acquired motor mechanism, repeated rather than represented.
Sorry, that's incorrect. Pure memory records a unique past event, such as one particular reading. Reciting the poem is habit memory.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Memory stored in the body and repeated, like a lesson learned by heart, is habit memory.

forms.stemHtml: What does Bergson mean by calling the body a "center of action"?

options.html: That the body produces inner pictures of the world
options.text: That the body produces inner pictures of the world
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Bergson denies that the body or brain produces representations. It receives influences and initiates actions.

options.html: That the body is the center of the physical universe
options.text: That the body is the center of the physical universe
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The body is a center of action in that it receives influences and initiates actions, not a cosmic center.

options.html: That it receives influences and initiates actions
options.text: That it receives influences and initiates actions
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The body is where influences are received and actions begin, and perception selects what bears on its possible actions.

options.html: That the body stores every past event as an image
options.text: That the body stores every past event as an image
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That's closer to pure memory, which Bergson doesn't locate in the body. The body receives influences and initiates actions.

title: Bergson's Duration
